# Dasarathajātaka (Ja 461)

**ID:** Ja 461
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Dasarathajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul10.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dasarathajātaka* (Ja 461) is the Buddhist adaptation of the Rāma legend in the Pali Jātaka collection [Appleton 2010; Holt 2008]. In the frame story set at Jetavana, the Buddha recounts the tale to comfort a grief-stricken householder mourning the death of his father by demonstrating that wise men of old bore loss without sorrow [Winternitz 1933]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as Rāmapaṇḍita, son of King Dasaratha of Benares, alongside his brother Lakkhaṇa and sister Sītā [Holt 2008; Huynh 2016]. Following palace intrigues after the king grants a boon to a younger queen for her son Bharata, Rāma, Lakkhaṇa, and Sītā withdraw to the forest [Anālayo 2010; Holt 2008; Huynh 2016]. When King Dasaratha dies, Bharata seeks Rāma in exile, but Rāma refuses to return until his father's designated term is complete, granting his straw slippers to rule in his stead; at the conclusion, Rāma returns to reign with Sītā as his queen consort [Holt 2008; Huynh 2016]. Notably, the narrative omits the abduction of Sītā and the expedition to Laṅkā found in the classical Sanskrit epic [Eliot 1921; Holt 2008]. Scholars note that the canonical verses (*gāthā*) essentially comprise moral sayings on impermanence to console the bereaved rather than an epic narrative, the latter being elaborated in the prose commentary [Winternitz 1933; Appleton 2010].

Verses from the *Dasarathajātaka* share substantial thematic and textual parallels across Buddhist canonical literature. Curated parallels exist with the *Salla Sutta* (Snp 3.8), the *Mūgapakkhajātaka* (Ja 538), several Dharmapada and Udānavarga traditions including the Gāndhārī Dharmapada (G-Dhp 139–161, G3-Dhp 41–50), the Sanskrit Udānavarga (UV 1), and Chinese translations (T 210, T 212, and T 213).

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Passage-level parallels: G-Dhp 139–161 Jaravagga; G3-Dhp 41–50 Gāndhārī 3rd Dharmapada Verses 41–50; UV 1 Anityavarga; T 213.1 法集要頌經有為品第一; Uv Kg 1 Impermanency; T 212.1 無常品第一之一; Ja 538 Mūgapakkhajātaka; Snp 3.8 (PTS Snp 112) Salla Sutta; T 210.37 生死品法句經第三十七十有八章

**Sources**

- [Anālayo 2010] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Genesis of the Bodhisattva Ideal (2010) — Analysis of the adaptation of the Rāmāyaṇa tale into a Buddhist jātaka and Sītā's role as sister and wife.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravāda Buddhism (2010) — Identification of the Bodhisatta as the ancient hero Rāma enacting an episode from the Rāmāyaṇa.
- [Eliot 1921] Charles Eliot, Hinduism and Buddhism: An Historical Sketch, Vol. 2 (1921) — Note on the omission of the expedition to Laṅkā and Sītā being portrayed as Rāma's sister.
- [Holt 2008] John Clifford Holt, The Buddhist Viṣṇu: Religious Transformation, Politics, and Culture (2008) — Detailed summary of the jātaka plot, characters, comparison with Sanskrit recensions, and the slippers motif.
- [Huynh 2016] Trung Huynh, Early Development of Buddhism in the Red River Delta Basin (2016) — Narrative details regarding the king's succession, forest exile, and royal straw slippers.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, A History of Indian Literature, Vol. 2 (1933) — Analysis of the verse core as consolatory moral verses rather than an epic narrative.
